title: 9 Ways To Never Lose Control Of Your Class
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Anticipating the behavioral spike that typically precedes holiday break, Linsin offers three strategies to keep a class calm and academically focused through the final stretch before vacation: reviewing the classroom management plan more frequently, deliberately slowing down physically and vocally, and refusing to ease off academic rigor. He argues that a teacher's own pace and energy set the emotional temperature of the room, so slowing one's movements, speech, and reactions directly counteracts rising student excitability. He also pushes back on the instinct to lighten academic demands near a break, arguing that doing so signals to students that vacation has effectively already started and invites more misbehavior, not less. The piece frames maintained rigor and a calmer teacher presence, rather than any special holiday-specific trick, as what keeps a class's learning and behavior steady through the pre-break stretch.
points: Review the classroom management plan more frequently -- at least twice a week -- in the days leading up to a holiday break, erring toward more detail rather than less.
Deliberately slow your own movement, speech, and pacing before a break; a hyperactive, rushed teacher energy transfers directly to a hyperactive class.
Keep academic rigor and deadlines at full strength through the last day of school rather than easing off, since lowered expectations signal that vacation has already begun.
Seasonal projects and activities are fine, but the standard for quality work should keep rising, not fall, as a break approaches.
quotes: Misbehavior tends to increase as we edge closer to holiday break. It’s a phenomenon as old as Santa and just as predictable.
Whenever you’re in doubt about what to do in response to increased misbehavior, always and first double-down on your classroom management plan.
Moving fast, talking fast, and rushing through lessons and routines always causes worsening behavior.
Students take their cue from you. Your energy determines the energy in the room. The more hyperactive and tense they are, the more relaxed and unhurried you should become.
But this signals to students that vacation starts before vacation—if you get my snow drift.
